Management of Intracranial Tumors

  • Cushing's triad = high systolic BP (wide pulse pressure), low HR, low/irregular RR. 432
Slide 3

CLASSIFICATION

How We Classify Intracranial Tumors

By origin

By biological behavior

By molecular profile

Primary (arising from brain, meninges, nerves, or pituitary) vs. secondary / metastatic (spread from a systemic cancer).

WHO CNS grade 1–4 reflects histology plus molecular markers — grade 1 is slow-growing/curable with resection, grade 4 is aggressive and infiltrative.

The 2021 WHO classification integrates markers (IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, MGMT methylation) alongside histology to guide prognosis and therapy.

Slide 5

CLASSIFICATION

Metastatic Disease & Age/Location Patterns

Metastatic brain tumors

Age & location patterns

  • The most common intracranial tumor overall in adults — more frequent than any primary CNS tumor.
  • Common primaries: lung, breast, melanoma, renal cell, colorectal.
  • Classically multiple lesions at the gray–white matter junction.
  • Management depends heavily on the number of lesions and systemic disease control.
  • Pediatric: predominantly infratentorial
    • Medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma, ependymoma
  • Adult: predominantly supratentorial
    • Glioma, meningioma, metastasis, primary CNS lymphoma

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Initial Clinical Assessment

History

Examination

  • Headache red flags: new, progressive, worse lying flat/with Valsalva, wakes from sleep
  • New-onset seizure
  • Progression and tempo of any focal deficit
  • Cognitive/personality change reported by family
  • Known systemic cancer (risk of metastasis)
  • Full neurological exam — mental status, cranial nerves, motor, sensory, cerebellar, gait
  • Fundoscopy for papilledema
  • Formal visual field testing
  • Cognitive screening when indicated
  • Vital signs — assess for Cushing triad

Slide 7

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Imaging & Adjunct Studies

CT head (non-contrast ± contrast)

First-line if acute presentation — confirms a mass lesion, assesses for hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, and herniation risk.

MRI brain with & without contrast

Definitive characterization and surgical planning; add advanced sequences (perfusion, spectroscopy) as needed.

Endocrine labs

For sellar/parasellar lesions — full anterior pituitary panel ± visual fields before intervention.

CSF studies

Cytology if leptomeningeal spread or CNS lymphoma suspected — only after imaging excludes a lumbar puncture contraindication (mass effect/risk of herniation).

Systemic work-up

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis ± tumor markers when a metastasis is suspected and no known primary is identified.

DIAGNOSTIC WORKUP

Getting a Tissue Diagnosis

Imaging suggests a diagnosis; histology (plus molecular testing) confirms it and drives adjuvant treatment.

Stereotactic biopsy

Open resection

For deep, eloquent, or multifocal lesions where resection carries high risk — obtains tissue with minimal morbidity.

Preferred when safely achievable — provides diagnosis and simultaneous therapeutic debulking/cytoreduction.

Intra-operative frozen section

Molecular markers

Rapid preliminary diagnosis in theatre to help guide the extent of resection in real time.

IDH mutation, 1p/19q co-deletion, and MGMT promoter methylation refine glioma diagnosis, prognosis, and chemosensitivity.

Management of Intracranial Tumors

Notes

Tissue Diagnosis & Surgical Principles

CORE PRINCIPLE: MAXIMUM SAFE RESECTION
Remove as much tumor as possible without unacceptable neurological deficit — not simply maximum resection. Always balance the benefit of greater removal against risk to eloquent cortex and critical structures (tumor in or near motor cortex may limit resection).
Notes

What surgery can provide

Tissue diagnosis·Debulking / resection·Relief of mass effect·Treatment of life- threatening complications

Intracranial Tumors: Management

THE ONE EXCEPTION: PRIMARY CNS LYMPHOMA
We aim for resection in every tumor except primary CNS lymphoma. It is highly chemo-/radiosensitive, so the usual approach is biopsy, not major resection.

Slide 9

ACUTE COMPLICATIONS

Managing Raised ICP — Medical Measures

Head position & ventilation

Osmotherapy

Elevate head of bed to 30°; maintain normocapnia (avoid hypercapnia, brief hyperventilation only as a bridge in impending herniation)

Mannitol or hypertonic saline draw free water out of brain tissue and reduce ICP acutely

Corticosteroids

Fluids & sedation

Dexamethasone reduces vasogenic edema around tumors (especially metastases) — not for cytotoxic edema

Avoid hypotonic fluids and hypotension; adequate analgesia/sedation limits ICP surges

Management of Intracranial Tumors

  • Frontal tumour surrounded by massive brain oedema → dexamethasone (vasogenic oedema). 438 ×2
  • Most potent and fastest way to lower ICP → controlled hyperventilation (only briefly, as a bridge). 437
  • Treatment of raised ICP → head elevation (not flexion, lateral position or head-down). 429 ×2

Slide 10

ACUTE COMPLICATIONS

Managing Raised ICP — Surgical Measures

External ventricular drain (EVD)

Diverts CSF for obstructive hydrocephalus; also allows direct ICP monitoring and therapeutic drainage.

Decompressive craniectomy

Removes a bone flap to give swollen brain room to expand — considered when medical measures fail or herniation is imminent.

Emergent tumor debulking

Urgent surgical resection when a tumor itself is causing acute deterioration or herniation — diagnosis and treatment combined.

Invasive ICP monitoring

Guides ongoing therapy in the critical care setting when the clinical exam is unreliable (e.g. sedated patient).

  • 60-year-old, progressive left-sided weakness (arm > leg) over 3 months + left UMN facial palsy, normal speech → right frontal glioblastoma (progressive = tumour; sudden = stroke). 434 ×2
  • Seizure + enhancing lesion of the left inferior frontal lobe → difficulty in expression (Broca). 437
  • Tumour patient collapses with high ICP — the pressure–volume curve → keyed "shifts to the right" (he is on the steep part: a small extra volume causes a large rise). 438

MeasureWhen / why
EVD (external ventricular drain)Especially with hydrocephalus.

Invasive ICP monitoringWhen indicated.
Slide 11

ACUTE COMPLICATIONS

Seizure Management

Established seizures

Prophylaxis & emergencies

  • Anti-epileptic drugs (AEDs) are started after a tumor-related seizure has occurred.
  • Levetiracetam is commonly favored — minimal drug interactions, available IV.
  • Choice is individualized around drug interactions with chemotherapy/steroids and side-effect profile.
  • Routine prophylactic AEDs are not recommended for patients who have never seized — guidelines reserve them for those with a seizure history.
  • Status epilepticus is a medical emergency: secure airway, IV benzodiazepine first line, then a loading AED; involve critical care early.

Management of Intracranial Tumors

10

Notes

Seizure

1 Protect airway Airway / ABC first·2 Terminate the seizure IV benzodiazepine: short-acting, first line·3 Prevent recurrence Load a longer-acting AED (e.g., phenytoin)
PROPHYLAXIS
A brain tumor alone, without a prior seizure, does not automatically mean chronic AED therapy. Perioperative AED use depends on the clinical and surgical circumstances.
Slide 12

ACUTE COMPLICATIONS

Other Emergencies to Recognize

Hydrocephalus

Intratumoral hemorrhage

Herniation syndromes

Obstructive (tumor blocking CSF pathway) vs. communicating (impaired CSF absorption) — both may need urgent CSF diversion.

Certain tumors (metastatic melanoma, renal cell, choriocarcinoma; high-grade glioma) bleed spontaneously, causing sudden deterioration.

Uncal (CN III palsy, contralateral hemiparesis), central (bilateral decline), and tonsillar (respiratory arrest) — recognize early warning signs.

Management of Intracranial Tumors

11

Notes

Hydrocephalus

TypeMechanismManagement
ObstructiveTumor blocks the CSF pathwayUrgent CSF diversion — EVD
CommunicatingImpaired CSF absorptionMay also need urgent CSF diversion — EVD
Notes

Herniation and hemorrhage

HERNIATION SYNDROME
A tumor can cause herniation through severe mass effect / raised ICP. Presentation and emergency ICP management are the same as herniation from other lesions; only the cause differs. Intratumoral hemorrhage can precipitate it acutely.
SILENT, THEN SUDDEN
Gliomas may grow very large and infiltrate deep structures before causing major symptoms. A patient may be walking and neurologically stable, then deteriorate abruptly from acute intratumoral bleeding.

TREATMENT

A Multidisciplinary Approach

Treatment decisions for intracranial tumors are made by a tumor board — neurosurgery, neuro-oncology, radiation oncology, neuropathology, and neuroradiology — weighing tumor biology against the patient’s functional status and goals.

Slide 14

TREATMENT — SURGERY

Surgical Resection: Goals & Techniques

Goal: maximal safe resection — removing as much tumor as possible while preserving neurological function.

Extent of resection

Image-guided neuronavigation

Gross total vs. subtotal resection is a key prognostic factor, especially in glioma.

MRI-based intra-operative "GPS" for the tumor and adjacent eloquent structures.

Awake craniotomy

Intra-operative MRI & mapping

Real-time language/motor testing during resection near eloquent cortex.

Confirms extent of resection and functional boundaries during surgery itself.

Endoscopic approaches

Minimally invasive corridor for sellar/skull base tumors (e.g. endonasal transsphenoidal).

Management of Intracranial Tumors

13

Notes

Surgical adjuncts (increase extent and safety of resection)

AdjunctUse
Awake craniotomyOperating near eloquent cortex.
Endoscopic approachesIncluding endonasal procedures for selected lesions.
NeuronavigationImage guidance.
Intraoperative neuromonitoringMonitors function during resection.
Intraoperative MRIChecks for residual tumor during surgery. Useful when greater resection is desired, but time-consuming.
Slide 15

TREATMENT — RADIOTHERAPY

Radiotherapy: Types & Indications

Fractionated external-beam RT (EBRT)

Standard adjuvant treatment for high-grade gliomas, delivered in daily fractions over several weeks to limit normal-tissue toxicity

Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS)

Single/few high-precision fractions (Gamma Knife, CyberKnife, LINAC-based) for small lesions — metastases, meningiomas, vestibular schwannomas

Whole-brain radiotherapy (WBRT)

Considered for multiple brain metastases or diffuse leptomeningeal disease, balanced against neurocognitive side effects

Proton beam therapy

Sharper dose fall-off spares surrounding tissue — particularly valuable in pediatric and skull-base tumors

Slide 16

TREATMENT — SYSTEMIC THERAPY

Chemotherapy & Targeted / Systemic Therapy

Temozolomide + radiotherapy

Bevacizumab

The Stupp protocol — concurrent chemoradiation followed by adjuvant temozolomide is standard of care for glioblastoma.

Anti-VEGF antibody used in recurrent glioblastoma; also reduces vasogenic edema and steroid dependence.

Targeted & immunotherapy

Hormonal / medical therapy

BRAF inhibitors for BRAF-mutant tumors; immunotherapy and vaccine trials are active areas of investigation.

Dopamine agonists (e.g. cabergoline) can shrink prolactinomas medically, often avoiding surgery altogether.

Intracranial Tumors: Management

Slide 18

Key Takeaways

  • Classify by origin (primary vs. metastatic) and biological grade — this frames prognosis and treatment intensity.
  • Assessment combines a focused history/exam with MRI and, when needed, tissue diagnosis.
  • Raised ICP, seizures, hydrocephalus, and hemorrhage are the acute complications to anticipate and treat promptly.
  • Treatment is multidisciplinary: surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy are complementary, not competing, tools.
  • The right combination — and sequence — of modalities depends on tumor type, location, and the patient in front of you.

Management of Intracranial Tumors

17

Slide 19

CASE EXAMPLE 1

Glioblastoma — A Management Pathway

Presentation

A patient presents with progressive focal neurological symptoms. MRI was obtained for further work-up.

Imaging & Workup

  • MRI: a thick, irregular ring-enhancing mass with a necrotic center and surrounding vasogenic edema
  • Started on dexamethasone for edema; levetiracetam only if a seizure occurs
  • Stereotactic biopsy confirms IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (WHO grade 4)

Management

  • Maximal safe resection with intra-operative mapping given eloquent location
  • Concurrent chemoradiation followed by adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp protocol)
  • Ongoing MRI surveillance for recurrence

Axial post-contrast T1 MRI: a thick, irregularly ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis and extensive surrounding edema — the classic glioblastoma appearance.

Ring-enhancing lesion + necrosis in an adult → think high-grade glioma; treatment sequencing follows the Stupp protocol.

Management of Intracranial Tumors

18

  • Intra-axial heterogeneous enhancing lesion in the right premotor gyrus → high-grade primary brain tumour. 437 ×2
Ring-enhancing lesion + necrosis in an adult → think high-grade glioma; treatment follows the Stupp protocol.
Slide 20

CASE EXAMPLE 2

Pituitary Macroadenoma — Choosing a Pathway

Presentation

A patient presents with amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and progressive bitemporal visual field loss.

Imaging & Workup

  • MRI: a sellar mass with suprasellar extension abutting the optic chiasm
  • Markedly elevated serum prolactin, consistent with a prolactin-secreting adenoma
  • Formal visual field testing confirms bitemporal hemianopia

Management

  • First-line: dopamine agonist therapy (e.g. cabergoline) — often shrinks the tumor and restores vision medically
  • Reserve endoscopic transsphenoidal resection for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy
  • Serial prolactin levels and visual fields to monitor response

Coronal post-contrast MRI: a sellar/suprasellar mass elevating and closely applied to the optic chiasm.

Not every sellar mass goes straight to surgery — a prolactinoma is treated medically first.

Management of Intracranial Tumors

19

  • Pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm (visual loss + disturbed menses) → bitemporal hemianopia. 437 ×6
Not every sellar mass goes straight to surgery — a prolactinoma is treated medically first.

Mastery Checklist

Classify by origin (primary vs secondary) and behavior (grade 1-4; IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT for gliomas).
1

2
